content: The analysis focused on cases of isoniazid-resistant tuberculosis (Hr-TB) and evaluated treatment regimens based on various factors, including the presence or absence of specific genetic mutations (katG and inhA promoter mutations), the use of normal or high-dose isoniazid, and the effectiveness of other drugs such as ethambutol, pyrazinamide, or injectable agents. It also considered patient characteristics such as prior TB treatment, extensive disease, HIV status (with or without antiretroviral therapy), age (children aged 0–14 years), and comorbidities like diabetes. The outcomes of interest included treatment success (defined as cure or completion of therapy), treatment failure or relapse, mortality, adverse reactions to anti-TB medications (categorized by severity, type, and organ system affected), and the development of additional drug resistance. Relapse was defined as the recurrence of disease within two years after successful treatment completion. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that approximately 10% of all TB cases are isoniazid-resistant without concurrent rifampicin resistance. While the impact of Hr-TB on treatment outcomes is less severe than multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), failure and relapse rates in randomized trials of first-line therapy are around 12–13%. A systematic review found that patients with Hr-TB had significantly higher rates of failure and relapse compared to those with drug-susceptible TB. To guide evidence review for Hr-TB treatment, the WHO expert panel developed a series of PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions. The outcomes analyzed included treatment success, failure/relapse, mortality, adverse drug reactions, and the acquisition of rifampicin resistance. Data were primarily drawn from a 2016 systematic review and updated until February 2016. Studies included cohorts with at least 20 Hr-TB patients or randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Patient-level data were standardized and analyzed based on treatment regimens grouped by key components (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, fluoroquinolones, and streptomycin) and treatment duration (6 months or longer). The analysis included data from 5,537 patients across 33 databases, with 5,418 patients having sufficient information for inclusion. Only 2% of the patients were children, precluding a specific analysis for this group. Treatment success was marginally higher with 6-month regimens containing rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide (6REZ) compared to longer regimens (7–9 months), though the benefit was not statistically significant when a single large study was excluded. Adding isoniazid to the regimen did not show additional benefit. The duration of treatment was not associated with a significant difference in the acquisition of rifampicin resistance. The use of fluoroquinolones (FQ) was associated with higher odds of treatment success when pyrazinamide was used for less than four months, although the comparator group also had high success rates. Fluoroquinolones were linked to lower mortality and reduced acquisition of rifampicin resistance. However, the addition of streptomycin (S) did not improve outcomes, and shorter durations of pyrazinamide (<4 months) were consistently associated with worse outcomes, even when streptomycin was included. In conclusion, 6REZ regimens appear to achieve high treatment success rates in Hr-TB patients. The addition of fluoroquinolones may reduce mortality and the risk of rifampicin resistance, potentially increasing success rates even when pyrazinamide is used for less than four months. This could help mitigate the hepatotoxicity associated with prolonged pyrazinamide use. However, the use of streptomycin did not demonstrate improved outcomes. Patients with extensive disease or additional drug resistance may benefit from extended treatment durations or the inclusion of fluoroquinolones or other agents.
